title: SaaS Compliance Proof for Buyers: What to Show
summary: What enterprise buyers accept as SaaS compliance proof: the evidence pack, what SOC 2 and ISO 27001 do and don't show, and how to keep answers consistent.
body_markdown:
Enterprise buyers accept compliance proof when it is independent, current and scoped to the exact service they are buying. A logo on your security page is a claim. A dated SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certificate, a recent penetration-test summary, a data processing agreement and consistent questionnaire answers are evidence. The vendors that close security reviews quickly keep all of it in one maintained place and answer from it every time. With Skypher, we automate that last step: answering questionnaires from your approved knowledge base, and publishing the proof in a Trust Center your buyers can open themselves.

## TL;DR


- Buyers want verifiable third-party evidence, not badges.[83% of enterprise buyers require SOC 2](https://technologymatch.com/blog/what-tech-vendors-must-know-about-concerns-about-data-protection) from SaaS vendors before contract signature, according to a 2025 industry article.
- A report only counts if its entity, product, period and exceptions match the service being bought.
- Review depth follows data sensitivity, so the proof you owe a buyer changes with what your product touches.
- Keep one dated master set of answers and artifacts, and every new questionnaire becomes a mapping exercise.
- Publishing the evidence in a Trust Center lets buyers self-serve before the first questionnaire arrives.

## What buyers mean by compliance proof


Compliance proof is evidence a buyer can check without taking your word for it. That is the line security teams draw. One way to describe it is three classes of claim: self-attested statements, documents shared only under NDA, and independent annual certifications by a named third party on a dated, recurring cycle.[Caspio's 2026 article on vendor claims](https://www.caspio.com/blog/reading-vendor-compliance-claims/) also advises confirming that the plan being purchased falls inside the certification's scope.


The weight buyers place on this is large. The same[TechnologyMatch article](https://technologymatch.com/blog/what-tech-vendors-must-know-about-concerns-about-data-protection) reports a study of 2,600+ organizations across 12 countries in which 98% said external privacy certifications influence buying decisions. It also cites a State of Trust report finding that SOC 2 Type II holders closed enterprise deals 35% faster.


For a sales director or solution engineer, this changes the job. The goal is not to have a certificate. The goal is to hand the buyer's security team the right artifact on the first request, with the scope already explained.


## The evidence pack buyers ask for


Most enterprise security reviews ask for the same set of documents.[Talk Think Do's guide for software vendors](https://talkthinkdo.com/guides/legal-and-contracts/enterprise-buyer-security-evidence-software-vendors/) groups them into three tiers, and a[B2B News UK procurement checklist](https://www.b2b-news.uk/the-exact-procurement-checklist-to-get-a-saas-security-audit-greenlit-in-a-month) describes a similar first request. Combined, a practical pack looks like this:


Tier Artifact What the buyer checks


Security Master questionnaire answers Access control, encryption, patching, logging, secure development, incident response


Security SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certificate Scope, period, auditor, exceptions


Security Penetration-test summary Scope, date, tester, remediation status (the raw report is not shared)


Data protection Data processing agreement (DPA) Processor terms, transfer mechanism


Data protection Subprocessor and hosting list Regions, every third party touching data


Continuity Disaster recovery statement Tested recovery time and recovery point objectives


Commercial SLA and insurance certificates Availability commitments, cyber and indemnity cover


A DPA is the contract that sets how you process personal data on the buyer's behalf. A subprocessor is any third party you use that touches that data, such as a cloud host or an AI provider.


Two habits make the pack work. First, every item carries a date and an owner. Second, you offer the items in the order the buyer's reviewer reads them: the report or certificate first, the narrative answers second.


## What SOC 2, ISO 27001 and pen tests do and don't show


Each artifact proves something specific. Knowing the boundary helps you present it honestly and pre-empt follow-up questions.


- **SOC 2 Type 2.**[The cisin.com CISO guide](https://www.cisin.com/coffee-break/how-to-validate-a-software-vendor-s-security-certifications-a-ciso-s-go-no-go-guide-to-soc-2-and-iso-27001-evidence.html) says it shows controls operated effectively across a stated period, within the system description. The period typically runs six to twelve months and ends before signature.
- **ISO/IEC 27001.** It shows an information security management system was audited within a stated scope. It does not show that every control is strong.
- **Pen-test summary.** It shows issues found in a defined scope at a point in time.
- **Security questionnaire.** It shows your own statements, not independent verification.


Buyers read SOC 2 reports in a predictable order.[Normstone's review guide](https://normstone.com/insights/how-to-review-soc-2-report/) starts with the legal entity, service, product version and dates. It then checks Type 1 versus Type 2, which Trust Services Criteria are covered, the auditor's opinion and any qualification, excluded products or locations, and the controls the customer is expected to run. A Security-only report, for example, is not an opinion on availability or privacy.


If you are choosing between attestations, our guides on[SOC 2 Type 1 versus Type 2](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/soc-2-type-1-vs-type-2-differences) ,[ISO 27001 versus SOC 2](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/iso27001-vs-soc2-standards) and[SOC 2 requirements](https://skypher.co/post/soc2-requirements-saas-trust-en) walk through the trade-offs. If you are early in the process,[SOC 2 Type 1](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/soc-2-type-1-security-assurance) is a common first step toward a Type 2 report.


### Pass the entity-and-scope test before you send anything


The cisin.com guide frames assurance as a chain: entity match, scope match, period, exceptions and customer-side controls. If one link fails, the evidence does not hold for that service. Before you send a report, check that:


1. The legal entity on the report is the entity on the contract.
2. The product and environments in scope are the ones the buyer will use, including integrations.
3. The observation period is recent enough that a bridge letter, if you offer one, can cover the gap.
4. Any exceptions are explained with remediation.


Sending a report that fails this test costs you a round trip. Fixing the scope statement first costs you an afternoon.


## Match your proof to the buyer's risk


Buyers do not apply one standard to every vendor. The[University of Michigan's vendor security guidance](https://safecomputing.umich.edu/protect-the-u/protect-your-unit/third-party-vendor-security-compliance/include-it-security-privacy-vendor-contract) shows the logic. Low-sensitivity data needs no security review. Moderate-sensitivity data needs a signed Data Security Agreement or equivalent. High or restricted data needs that agreement plus a vendor security questionnaire. ISO or FedRAMP certification can substitute, and SOC 2 can too if it addresses the same risk factors. Documentation that covers only the underlying cloud hosting is not accepted.


[Rework's buyer framework](https://resources.rework.com/guides/saas-buying-framework/security-compliance-review) makes the same point from the procurement side: depth should follow the sensitivity of the data, not contract value. It also notes that review backlogs break when teams run the same 200-question questionnaire against every vendor.


For you, this means preparing three versions of the story:


- **Light review:** a short security overview, DPA and subprocessor list.
- **Standard review:** the above plus SOC 2 or ISO 27001 and a pen-test summary.
- **Elevated review:** everything, plus a completed standard questionnaire, a disaster recovery statement and a written breach-notification commitment.


Rework recommends a written 72-hour breach notification SLA that mirrors GDPR Article 33. Offering it unprompted answers a question certifications never do.


## Keep the evidence organized, dated and shareable


The most common proof failure is not a missing certificate. It is a stale or contradictory document.[Edilec's trust center guidance](https://edilec.com/blog/cyb-11050/saas-security-trust-center-evidence/) recommends that each artifact carry an owner, issuer, service scope, legal entities, regions, period, issue and expiry dates, confidentiality level and permitted recipients. It adds three practices:


- Assign review triggers: product changes, new regions, acquisitions, incidents, subprocessor or legal changes.
- Mark superseded documents instead of silently replacing them at the same link.
- Route changes from the content owner through security validation, legal and privacy before an accountable publisher releases them.


That is a document-control process, and it pays back every time a buyer asks. It is also where tooling matters. A Trust Center gives buyers a single place for reports, policies and subprocessor lists, gated where needed, so your sales team stops attaching PDFs to emails. Our[Trust Center](https://skypher.co/trust-center) is customizable for this purpose, and it sits alongside the questionnaire workflow so the evidence and the answers come from the same source.


For the technical side of the same trust conversation, this overview of[website security and customer trust](https://babylovegrowth.ai/blog/importance-website-security) is a good complement.


## Answer questionnaires the same way every time


Reports get you through the gate. Questionnaires are where deals slow down. Talk Think Do advises answering the whole common set once in a single maintained document, so each later questionnaire becomes a mapping exercise. It also stresses a dated version history, because reviewers notice when an answer contradicts one given six months earlier.


Three question families cause the most inconsistency:


- **Subprocessors.** List every one that handles personal data, with its role, location and data access.
- **Data location.** State the cloud provider, storage and processing regions, and any transfers outside the UK or EEA with the mechanism used.
- **AI services.** Buyers ask whether customer data is used for training, where inference happens and what retention the provider applies. Verify each answer against the provider's own terms.


Standard formats help. An[NHIMG guide to security questionnaires](https://nhimg.org/security-questionnaires-guide) notes that the 2026 SIG, released 19 September 2025, added references to ISO/IEC 42001 for AI. It also says CAIQ yes/no answers are useful only with comments explaining scope and whether the control belongs to the provider or the customer.


To learn the formats and the usual mistakes, read our guides on[answering security questionnaires](https://skypher.co/post/how-to-answer-security-questionnaires) and[responding to an RFP security questionnaire](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/how-to-respond-to-an-rfp) .

## Know which rules your buyers answer to


Compliance proof is shaped by the regulations your buyers face, even when those rules do not bind you directly.


- **EU financial services.**[DORA](https://vcisolite.com/blog/dora-compliance-us-saas-eu-financial-services) has applied since 17 January 2025 and binds EU financial entities rather than US software vendors. Its obligations reach you through contracts and questionnaires.
- **NIS2.**[Clarysec's procurement analysis](https://blog.clarysec.com/posts/secure-by-demand-software-procurement-iso-27001-nis2-dora-cra-gdpr/) notes that Article 21 requires supply chain security and that Article 23 sets 24-hour early warning and 72-hour notification for incidents. Expect asks about hosting locations, subprocessor change notices, patch SLAs and whether customer data trains AI.
- **GDPR.** Data processing terms and transfer mechanisms are standard requests. Our overview of[GDPR software compliance](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/gdpr-software-compliance-saas) covers the key actions.


Buyers also carry their own duties. Compliance with HIPAA, GDPR or COPPA creates obligations on the buyer's side too, such as configuration and consent handling, as the[NHIMG analysis](https://nhimg.org/articles/saas-vendor-compliance-signals-need-tighter-identity-due-diligence/) points out. Clear shared-responsibility statements in your answers save a follow-up call.

## FAQ


### What is the most common compliance proof SaaS buyers require?


SOC 2 is the most frequent request from US enterprise buyers. The[TechnologyMatch article](https://technologymatch.com/blog/what-tech-vendors-must-know-about-concerns-about-data-protection) cites 83% of enterprise buyers requiring it before signature, rising to 91% among companies with 5,000+ employees. ISO 27001 is the usual alternative, especially outside the US.


### Do we need SOC 2 to sell to enterprises?


Not always. Review depth depends on the data you will handle. Some buyer tiers accept a recent scan or pen-test summary plus a basic security policy, as the[SaaSfort evidence guide](https://saasfort.com/blog/security-evidence-package-saas-vendor-enterprise-2026) describes for growth-stage enterprises. For regulated buyers, SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 is the norm.


### How current does our evidence need to be?


A SOC 2 Type II covers a past observation period, so buyers look for a recent report and an explanation for any gap. Dating every artifact and replacing it on a schedule keeps you ahead of that question.


### Why do questionnaires still arrive if we have a certificate?


A certificate shows independent testing of a defined scope. A questionnaire covers areas a report may not, such as contract terms, subprocessors, data location and AI use. Consistent master answers make both quick to handle.
